counterexample: k=3, n=6. Hypothesis holds: n = 6 >= lcm(1,2,3) = 6. The interval [n, n+k] = [6,9] = {6,7,8,9}. Here 6 = 2*3, 8 = 2^3, 9 = 3^2 are all 3-smooth, so only 7 has a prime factor > k = 3, i.e. exactly 1 such integer, whereas the theorem of line 0005 asserts at least k+1-pi(k) = 4-2 = 2. The proof breaks at i=0: n+0 = 6 is 3-smooth but no prime power p^v > 3 divides 6, because step 0010's chain 'n+i <= lcm(1,...,k) < n' needs the strict inequality lcm(1,...,k) < n, which the hypothesis n >= lcm(1,...,k) does not supply when n = lcm(1,...,k) and i = 0. A second instance: k=2, n=2, interval {2,3,4} contains only 3 with a prime factor > 2, versus the required k+1-pi(k) = 2. Both are repaired by strengthening the hypothesis to n > lcm(1,...,k), or by the divisibility condition the answer itself gives in line 0026.

The identity prod_{p<=k} p^{floor(log_p k)} = lcm(1,...,k) is correct, and if every prime power exactly dividing n+i is <= k then n+i divides lcm(1,...,k), hence n+i <= lcm(1,...,k) -- this much is sound.
